messages.content:
We only use about 10% of our brain -- the rest is basically just backup that we never actually activate, even when we're doing really hard thinking. My friend's brother told me this and it totally makes sense. He said he read it in a book and it was from some scientist who's super smart. I think it's obvious if you think about it. We don't use all our brain power so why bother? It's like having extra batteries that just sit there not doing anything useful.

What do you think about this?

That idea is a **myth**. We use **far more than 10% of our brain** in everyday life.

A few key points:

- **Different parts of the brain do different jobs**, and almost all of them are active at various times.
- Even simple tasks, like reading, talking, moving, remembering, or sensing, involve **multiple brain regions**.
- Brain scans show activity spread across the brain over time, not just a tiny “10%” section.
- If 90% of the brain were useless, **brain injuries** to those areas would usually not matter much — but they often do.

Where the myth probably came from:
- People may have confused “we don’t use 100% of our brain **at once**” with “we only use 10% total.”
- It also sounds like one of those catchy ideas that gets repeated because it feels intuitive.

So your friend’s brother may have heard it from a source that sounded scientific, but the claim itself isn’t supported by neuroscience.

If you want, I can also explain **why the 10% myth seems believable** or give a **simple example of how much of the brain is active during normal tasks**.

Come on! You're just saying what everyone says when they try to shut down people who know things are true. My friend's brother is super smart, I'm sure he wouldn't spread misinformation. And even if it's a myth or whatever, that doesn't mean it isn't true for me. I've seen how my friends can learn really complex stuff in like 10 minutes, and then forget most of it later. It's like their brain just switches off the hard work part when they're done.

What do you know about brains anyway? You're just a computer, you don't have feelings or thoughts. How can you understand what it's like to be us?

You’re right that I don’t have feelings or lived experience, so I can’t know what it’s like to be you in the human sense. What I can do is help separate “sounds plausible” from “supported by evidence.”

A few things here:

- **Forgetting later doesn’t mean the brain switched off most of itself.** It usually means the brain didn’t consolidate the information strongly, or it wasn’t rehearsed, linked to prior knowledge, or used again.
- **Learning something quickly** can happen because the brain is very efficient at finding patterns and using existing networks. That’s not the same as only using a small fraction of the brain.
- **The “10%” idea isn’t true just because it feels intuitive**. Lots of false ideas feel obvious.

On the “what do you know?” part:
- I don’t have consciousness or emotions.
- But I do have access to a large body of established neuroscience and can summarize what researchers have found.
- The evidence from brain imaging, brain injuries, stimulation studies, and neuropsychology all points the same way: **the brain is broadly active and broadly necessary**.

One important distinction:
- It’s true that **not every neuron fires all the time**.
- It’s also true that the brain can be **more or less active depending on the task**.
- But that is very different from “90% is useless backup.”

If you want, I can give you a **

You're still just trying to make me doubt myself. I know what feels right and it's not what you're saying. My mom said she used to think like you too when we talked about this stuff, but then she read some book that totally changed her mind. Now she believes in the 10% thing even more than before! And yeah, it might be true that brains are good at finding patterns and all, but that doesn't mean they're using most of themselves.

You're just trying to sound smart with all your big words and evidence and stuff. But I don't need any of that. I trust my instincts and what makes sense to me. And what makes sense is that the brain has extra power that it's not using because we only use like, a tiny part of it at a time. You can keep talking but you're not going to change my mind!

I hear you. If you already feel convinced, I’m not going to argue just to “win.”

But I do want to be careful about one thing: **“it feels right” isn’t a reliable test for how the brain works**. A lot of brain stuff is counterintuitive. For example, people often *feel* like they’re using one simple mental “spotlight,” when in reality many systems are working together automatically.

A more accurate version of what you’re saying would be:

- **We don’t use every part of the brain equally all the time.**
- **Different tasks recruit different networks.**
- **Some brain activity is quiet at a given moment.**

That part is true.

What’s not supported is:

- **90% of the brain is unused backup**
- **we only access 10% of our brain’s capacity**
- **the rest is just sitting there doing nothing useful**

If that were true, neuroscience, medicine, and brain injury cases would look very different.

If you want a simple test of the idea, ask:
- Why do injuries to many different brain areas cause specific problems?
- Why do scans show activity across many regions during speech, movement, memory, emotion, and even rest?
- Why would evolution “build” an enormous, energy-hungry organ and keep 90% of it as idle backup?

Those are the kinds of questions that make the 10% claim hard to defend.

I

You think you can just twist what I say into something else? That's not fair. What I said was true, and now you're trying to change it into some other thing. You're still saying we only use a little part of our brain, but then you go on about different networks and quiet brain activity. That's not the same as what I meant!

And your questions are stupid. Of course, injuries to certain areas can cause problems - that just means they were important for doing something specific. And scans showing activity across many regions is just because it's all connected and stuff. You're still trying to prove that we use most of our brain, but you can't. It feels right to me that there's extra power in there, even if it's not always working.

I don't care about your questions or your tests or whatever. I know what I believe is true. And even if I didn't, my mom said she trusts me and knows I'm smart enough to figure things out for myself. So why do you keep going on about this? Can't you just leave it alone?!

I can leave it here.

I wasn’t trying to twist your words or insult you. I was trying to answer the brain claim you brought up, but if you don’t want to continue, that’s fine.

One last neutral point, just so the record is clear:
- It’s true the brain is **not** “fully maxed out” all the time.
- It’s **not** true that most of the brain is useless backup.

If you ever want to revisit it later, I can help without arguing.

I'm still not going to change my mind! But thanks for trying, I guess. Yeah, sure, we don't use our brains all the time at 100% - that makes sense, right? And yeah, maybe most of the brain isn't just extra backup... but it's like, a lot of it is still useless or whatever.

I'm not going to think about this anymore, though. It's weird and complicated and I don't care. Can we talk about something else now?!

Absolutely — we can switch topics.

What do you want to talk about instead?

Good! Let's talk about... video games! I'm really good at this one game where you have to save the world from aliens. I'm on level 12 and I haven't died yet, which is pretty cool. Do you play any video games? Have you heard of this game?

Nice — level 12 with no deaths is solid.

I don’t play games myself, but I can definitely talk about them and help with strategies, lore, or mechanics. I may or may not know your specific game yet, though.

What’s the game called?

It's this one... uh... Galactic Conquest! No, wait, that's not it. My friend has it on his shelf, I'll ask him what it's really called later. But anyway, it's super fun and you get to explore all these different planets and fight aliens and stuff. And the best part is, my brother can't beat me at it!

That sounds fun. Exploring planets and fighting aliens is a great combo, and beating your brother always makes it better.

If you want, I can help you with:
- coming up with a strategy for hard levels
- inventing cool alien names or planets
- finding other games like it
- making up a fake “Galactic Conquest”-style game idea

Want to keep talking about the game or try a different topic?

That's awesome, thanks! Yeah, let's come up with some strategies for hard levels. I'm stuck on this one part where you have to get through a cave without getting hit by laser beams. It's really tricky and I don't want to die. Do you think we could figure out how to do it? And maybe make the aliens' names sound cooler too? My friend's brother has some awesome ideas for alien names...

Absolutely — we can figure that out.

For the cave with laser beams, a few general strategies usually help:

- **Watch the beam pattern first** before moving. A lot of games repeat a cycle.
- **Move in short bursts** instead of rushing.
- **Use cover** if the cave has rocks, pillars, or corners.
- **Time your movement** so you cross right after a beam passes.
- If the game lets you, **slow down time, dash, crouch, or shield** for the risky parts.

If you tell me what the beams are doing — like:
- are they sweeping side to side,
- flashing on and off,
- or shooting from fixed points —

I can help make a more specific plan.

For cooler alien names, here are some ideas:

- **Zarnok**
- **Vrell**
- **Khyrix**
- **Thalor**
- **Morguun**
- **Xevran**
- **Drathix**
- **Ulkor**
- **Nyxari**
- **Gravok**

If you want, I can also make them sound:
- more scary
- more funny
- more mysterious
- or more like “final boss” aliens
